latent_mechanisms.display_name: Autoreactive B/T cell and autoantibody activity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Reactivation of rheumatoid autoimmunity with RF/ACPA-associated immune activation, antigen presentation, macrophage recruitment, and systemic flare potential.
Activated synovial macrophages, fibroblast-like synoviocytes, T cells, B cells, and neutrophil-rich effusions drive swollen painful joints, morning stiffness, and inflammatory synovial fluid.
Cytokine amplification from IL-6, TNF, IL-1, IL-17, and macrophage pathways drives CRP/ESR elevation, fever, fatigue, anemia of inflammation, and reactive thrombocytosis.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Extra-articular serosal and lung inflammatory activity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Systemic RA inflammation can flare as rheumatoid pleuritis, pleural effusion, pneumonitis, or acute exacerbation of RA-associated interstitial lung disease.
Persistent synovitis activates osteoclasts, matrix metalloproteinases, pannus invasion, and structural damage risk.
Baseline immunosuppression, glucocorticoid exposure, biologics, age, and lung disease shape infection risk, muted inflammatory markers, and respiratory reserve during a flare.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: RA autoimmunity sustains macrophage and fibroblast-like synoviocyte activation in involved joints.
Autoimmune reactivation amplifies TNF, IL-6, IL-1, and IL-17 pathways.
Systemic RA can involve pleura and lung parenchyma during flares, especially in seropositive or established disease.
Persistent synovitis drives erosive joint damage through pannus and osteoclast pathways.
Objective synovitis is the core clinical expression of an articular RA flare.
Synovial inflammation causes joint pain and tenderness.
Synovitis and effusion produce visible or palpable swelling.
Inflammatory arthritis prolongs morning stiffness.
Large-joint RA flares can produce drainable effusions that mimic septic arthritis or PJI.
Inflammatory RA effusions can have thousands to tens of thousands of leukocytes per microliter.
Active inflammatory effusions may be neutrophil-predominant, although cultures and crystal analysis remain diagnostic workup context.
MMP-3 is a synovial inflammation and joint-damage activity marker used in some RA cohorts.
IL-6 is a dominant driver of hepatic CRP production in active RA.
ESR rises with fibrinogen and immunoglobulin changes in systemic inflammatory RA activity.
Systemic RA flares may cause low-grade fever; high persistent fever should remain a mimic exposure for infection or autoinflammatory disease.
Qualitative fever history can reflect systemic inflammatory activity when exact temperature is absent.
Cytokine activity contributes to fatigue and malaise during RA flares.
Inflammation and glucocorticoid exposure can produce mild leukocytosis; marked leukocytosis remains a mimic exposure.
Reactive thrombocytosis tracks inflammatory burden.
Anemia of inflammation can accompany persistent systemic RA activity.
RF positivity supports RA biology but is not a short-term flare gauge and should not be used as presentation-only confirmatory evidence unless explicitly allowed.
Rheumatoid pleuritis can produce exudative pleural effusion.
Pleural effusion extent tracks serosal inflammation burden.
Pleural effusion, pneumonitis, or ILD exacerbation can cause dyspnea.
RA-associated pneumonitis or ILD exacerbation can show ground-glass opacities, but infection must remain a major mimic.
RA-ILD activity can become clinically visible during systemic flares.
Severe pulmonary RA activity may impair gas exchange.
Acute RA-ILD exacerbation or large effusion can progress to respiratory failure.
Uncontrolled synovitis raises structural damage and disability risk.
Age, steroids, biologics, JAK inhibitors, and comorbidity raise serious infection hazard during flare treatment.
Respiratory failure is the main short-term death pathway in severe systemic RA pulmonary flare.
Serious infection or missed infection increases mortality during immunosuppressive flare treatment.
Most RA flares have low short-term mortality; extreme systemic cytokine activity can contribute to organ-level risk.

axes.shape_free_text: Objective inflammatory arthritis burden, including tender/swollen joints or clinically active synovitis.
Subjective joint pain or tenderness during a flare.
Visible or palpable swelling from synovitis or effusion.
Duration of inflammatory morning stiffness.
Probability that an inflamed joint has an effusion large enough to aspirate or show clearly on ultrasound.
Inflammatory synovial-fluid leukocyte count in an RA effusion; can overlap septic arthritis cutoffs and must be interpreted with culture/crystal context.
Neutrophil fraction in inflammatory RA synovial fluid.
MMP-3 activity marker reflecting synovial inflammation and joint destruction biology in RA.
CRP elevation from IL-6-driven acute phase activity; may be muted by IL-6 blockade.
ESR elevation reflecting systemic inflammatory RA activity.
Usually normal or low-grade fever; marked fever should keep infection, Still disease, HLH/MAS, and other mimics competitive.
Qualitative fever or feverishness during systemic flare.
Fatigue, malaise, or systemic sickness feeling during inflammatory activity.
May be normal or mildly high from inflammation or glucocorticoids; leukopenia suggests drug toxicity, Felty syndrome, SLE, viral infection, or marrow disease.
Neutrophils may be normal or mildly high, especially with glucocorticoids.
Anemia of inflammation may accompany persistent systemic RA activity.
Reactive thrombocytosis may track inflammation; thrombocytopenia suggests alternative or comorbid processes.
RF positivity is a chronic RA context marker, not a short-term flare marker.
Rheumatoid pleuritis or systemic serositis activity producing pleural effusion.
Extent of pleural effusion from rheumatoid pleuritis or inflammatory serositis.
Dyspnea from pleural effusion, pneumonitis, or RA-ILD exacerbation.
Ground-glass opacity burden during RA pneumonitis or ILD exacerbation; infection remains a key mimic.
RA-associated ILD activity or acute exacerbation extent.
Oxygen saturation can fall in severe pulmonary RA flare.
Respiratory failure risk from RA-ILD exacerbation, pneumonitis, or large pleural effusion.
Serious infection risk from immunosuppression and missed infectious mimics during flare management.
Hazard of structural damage or function loss from persistent uncontrolled inflammatory synovitis.
Disease-specific lifespan hazard for RA systemic flare, mainly mediated by respiratory failure, serious infection, severe frailty, and rare extreme systemic inflammation.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Tender/swollen joint burden and visible swelling usually move together in active synovitis.
Morning stiffness tends to rise with inflammatory arthritis activity.
Swollen large joints are more likely to have drainable effusions.
CRP and ESR often track systemic inflammatory burden, with ESR lagging and being affected by anemia and immunoglobulins.
Reactive thrombocytosis can accompany sustained acute-phase activity.
Sustained inflammatory activity may reduce hemoglobin through anemia of inflammation.
Rheumatoid pleural effusion can cause dyspnea.
Active ILD extent can lower oxygen saturation.
Severe RA-ILD exacerbation can progress to respiratory failure.
Respiratory failure is a plausible short-term death pathway in severe systemic RA pulmonary flare.
Serious infection or missed infection while immunosuppressed can dominate short-term risk.
Longstanding uncontrolled synovitis drives structural damage and disability.

treatments.clinical_role: Rapid suppression of systemic inflammatory and synovitis activity while longer-acting DMARD changes take effect.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Glucocorticoids rapidly suppress cytokine and acute-phase activity.
Glucocorticoids reduce synovitis and joint swelling.
Systemic steroids increase infection risk in susceptible hosts.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: When infection is likely, immunosuppression can worsen outcome and an infectious manifold should remain competitive.

treatments.clinical_role: Local control for a dominant inflamed joint after infection and crystal disease have been reasonably excluded.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Local steroid reduces joint inflammation.
Effusion and swelling can improve after local inflammation is suppressed.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Injecting an infected joint is unsafe; culture/clinical context must be handled outside disease ranking.

treatments.clinical_role: Symptom relief for pain and stiffness when renal, bleeding, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal context allows.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: NSAIDs reduce inflammatory pain but do not reshape the autoimmune manifold enough for sustained control.

treatments.clinical_role: Rebuilds disease-modifying control after undertreatment or inadequate csDMARD exposure.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Methotrexate reduces RA autoimmune and synovial activity over weeks.
Sustained disease modification lowers structural damage hazard.

treatments.clinical_role: Lower-intensity disease modification or combination csDMARD support.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Effect is slower and milder than biologic or JAK inhibition.

treatments.clinical_role: Biologic cytokine control for active synovitis and inflammatory burden when context supports use.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: TNF blockade reduces systemic and synovial cytokine activity.
TNF blockade increases serious and granulomatous infection susceptibility.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active or high-probability infection weakens biologic benefit.

treatments.clinical_role: Suppresses IL-6-driven acute-phase and systemic inflammatory activity; CRP may become pharmacologically muted.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: IL-6 blockade directly reduces IL-6 acute-phase signaling.
CRP can fall because IL-6 signaling is blocked, even if other inflammatory axes remain active.
Biologic immunosuppression increases infection risk and can mask CRP response.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: High infection risk or active infection changes the expected net vector field.

treatments.clinical_role: Broad cytokine pathway suppression for active RA flare biology.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: JAK inhibition suppresses multiple cytokine pathways involved in flare amplification.
JAK inhibition increases serious infection and viral reactivation risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Infection risk and frailty strongly shape the net effect.

treatments.clinical_role: T-cell costimulation modulation for autoimmune synovitis and some systemic RA activity contexts.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Abatacept dampens T-cell costimulation and downstream synovitis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Infectious mimics and immunosuppression context constrain use.

treatments.clinical_role: B-cell depletion for seropositive or refractory autoimmune RA activity.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: B-cell depletion reduces autoantibody-supporting RA immune activity over weeks.
B-cell depletion can raise infection risk, especially with hypogammaglobulinemia or prior immunosuppression.

treatments.clinical_role: Support gas exchange during pulmonary RA flare while immune-directed treatment takes effect.

trajectory_modifications.clinical_rationale: Supplemental oxygen or ventilatory support directly improves oxygenation when hypoxemia is present.
Respiratory support reduces immediate hypoxemic risk but does not treat the underlying inflammatory lung process.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Supportive respiratory care matters most when respiratory failure risk is active.

present.clinical_rationale: Established seropositive RA raises the prior that a compatible inflammatory arthritis episode is an RA flare.
Medication interruption or undertreatment can unmask synovitis and acute-phase activity.
Known RA-ILD increases pulmonary flare severity and respiratory reserve risk.

older_adult.clinical_rationale: Older age and frailty raise complications from infection, pulmonary disease, and immunosuppression.

present.clinical_rationale: Immunosuppression shapes infection risk and can alter inflammatory marker expression.
IL-6 blockade can mute CRP and fever even when non-CRP disease activity is present.

supportive_care.clinical_role: Obtains synovial fluid cell count, crystals, and cultures when a large effusion could be septic arthritis, crystal disease, Lyme arthritis, or PJI mimic.
Preserves diagnostic safety because RA flare and infection can share high CRP, synovial leukocytosis, and joint swelling.
Maintains range of motion and function after acute pain and inflammation are controlled.
Monitor oxygenation and imaging when dyspnea, pleural effusion, or ILD activity is present.
